narrative: The model estimated a 57.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—slightly more likely than not—so your application was denied based on that prediction. The strongest influence was your LSAT score of 39, which actually helped your case because it is above the accepted-student average of about 37.2 and pushed the prediction toward passing. However, the next two most important factors both pushed toward failure: your undergraduate GPA of 2.80, below the accepted average of 3.23, and your third-year class standing in the fourth decile, below the accepted average near 5.8. Together, those academic signals outweighed the positive LSAT signal and drove the predicted failure probability above the denial threshold. To strengthen a future application, focus on raising your academic record through additional rigorous coursework or a graduate-level program, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can achieve a clearly stronger score. Ask an admissions advisor how to present any extenuating circumstances, and apply to programs that review applicants holistically rather than relying heavily on predictive screening.
